## What Chapter 7 does with this

The terminal is now honest and ugly: three kinds of content distinguished by
colour, across two file descriptors, in a display that cannot redraw.

The display vocabulary is in place, with response identity still to resolve. Chunks carry a kind, so a consumer can
route them. Chunks carry a part id, so a consumer can group them into one
widget. Parts finalize with the same id, so a consumer can replace streamed
approximations with the authoritative version. Clients attach observers without importing GUI behavior into the core.
Persistent widget identity and connection lifetime belong to the GUI chapter.

A GUI's requirements list, written as a seam before anyone wrote a line of the
GUI. Chapter 7 cashes it in.

---

# Chapter 7: Everything Is an Artifact

The terminal from Chapter 6 is honest and ugly: three streams in three
colours, wrapping at terminal width, no memory of what scrolled past.
A tool the human cannot comfortably watch is a tool the human cannot
steer, and steering is the entire safety argument. This chapter builds
one reusable component, wires it to the agent through a WebSocket, and
the agent never learns the GUI exists.

---

## TL;DR

The agent writes observations. The GUI reads them. The core has no GUI
import, dependency or display configuration. Chapter 5's public observation
and input seams connect the two. GUI and WebSocket implementation live in a
separate optional Go module; the application constructs one Ensemble and one
Agent for both terminal and browser.

### The observer, extended

Two tool-boundary observation types, plus turn-end display progress:

```go
// Shared vocabulary in internal/common; public aliases expose it to clients.
// Keep observation names distinct from mailbox reports and stored events.

// ToolDispatched reports the boundary before handler execution.
type ToolDispatched struct {
    // CallID correlates execution with its requested call.
    CallID string          `json:"call_id"`
    // Name identifies the selected tool.
    Name   string          `json:"name"`
    // Input preserves raw arguments without interpreting them.
    Input  json.RawMessage `json:"input"`
}

// ToolFinished reports a wait result, including late reports after interrupt.
type ToolFinished struct {
    // CallID identifies the call that returned this result.
    CallID  string  `json:"call_id"`
    // Result is bounded text; full job output remains recoverable.
    Result  string  `json:"result"`
    // IsError distinguishes failed tool output.
    IsError bool    `json:"is_error"`
}

// TurnEnded is progress, not a reliable request acknowledgement.
type TurnEnded struct {
    // Text is the final reply, excluding intermediate tool narration.
    Text  string `json:"text"`
    // Error is a safe diagnostic for a failed or interrupted turn.
    Error string `json:"error,omitempty"`
}

func (ToolDispatched) observation() {}
func (ToolFinished) observation()   {}
func (TurnEnded) observation()      {}
```

`ToolDispatched` fires before execution. `ToolFinished` reports the returned
tool wait result; a job can still be running after that wait. Preserve later
real job reports. Together with `PartDelta`, `PartFinal` and `StateChanged`,
these observations show the turn's progress. Ensemble identifies the source
Agent when notifying clients; tools do not acquire a copied Agent identity
or a GUI parent. Reliable request replies remain separate from display progress.

### The wire

A WebSocket server subscribes through Ensemble's public identified observer
interface and fans out JSON to connected clients. Durable content comes from
the Agent's history; transient deltas and state observations complete the view.
These are examples of individual envelopes, not one complete conversation:

```json
{"type":"part_delta","part_id":3,"kind":"text","chunk":"Hello"}
{"type":"state_changed","from":"input_pending","to":"in_flight"}
{"type":"tool_dispatched","call_id":"tc_1","name":"read_file","input":{"path":"main.go"}}
{"type":"tool_finished","call_id":"tc_1","result":"package main...","is_error":false}
{"type":"part_final","part_id":3,"part":{"type":"text","text":"The file contains..."}}
{"type":"turn_ended","text":"The file contains..."}
```

Client messages:

```json
{"type":"subscribe"}
{"type":"prompt","text":"Run the tests"}
{"type":"hint","text":"Skip the slow ones"}
{"type":"interrupt"}
{"type":"pause"}
{"type":"unpause"}
```

### Reconnection

A client subscribes. The server sends two things: a window of recent
events from the event log (the last hour or last 100 renderable
events, whichever is larger), and the accumulated partial content for
anything currently streaming. The client renders the event history as
finalized Artifacts, replays the partial content to catch up to the
live stream position, then switches to live delivery. A fresh
connection and a reconnection after an hour use the same path. The
agent does not pause, restart, or notice.

No client cursor or client sequence numbers. The event log has its own ordering.
On each live observation, the hub checks for new entries since its captured
Seq and sends their renderable content alongside the streaming content. That
internal frontier is not a cursor supplied by the browser. The client never
parses SSE frames. Content messages carry an artifact or call identity and a
payload ready to render; status messages carry the effective state.

### The Artifact

Everything the agent produces is an Artifact: a widget that streams,
then finalizes.

| artifact | streaming format | finalized rendering |
|---|---|---|
| thinking | markdown (dim) | collapsible |
| chat | markdown | the response |
| tool call params | JSON (parameters as they arrive) | name + abbreviated args |
| tool result | n/a (not streamed) | type-specific: diff for edit_file, results for search_files |
| user message | n/a | the prompt |

One component, `ArtifactScroll`, manages the list. It receives
WebSocket messages, creates or updates Artifacts by display identity, streams
chunks through the format-appropriate renderer, and replaces them
with finalized HTML when the part completes. Different visual
treatment comes from CSS classes, not separate component types.

Two rules govern what a card is allowed to do with that text, and both
were broken in the first edition's implementation until its Chapter 13 audit.

Build the card with `textContent`. Never assemble it by interpolating
values into `innerHTML`. A tool call's name and arguments carry text the
agent did not write: a filename, a fetched URL, the contents of a file
it just read. Markup arriving inside any of those executes in the page.
This is the prompt-injection surface from the security chapter, reaching
the user through the renderer rather than through the model, and it is
easy to miss because the insecure version is shorter and reads better.

Cap what a card displays, and keep the remainder reachable. A cap with
an ellipsis and no affordance deletes the rest permanently for a reader
who cannot scroll past it. Put the full value in a `title` attribute or
behind an expander, so the limit governs the display instead of the
information.

### TTS

Two channels. **Auto-speak** fires during streaming: full text for
thinking and chat, an abbreviated summary for tool calls ("read file:
main.go, line 42"), silence for tool results. **On-demand** via a
speaker icon on every Artifact card, speaking the full accessible
text on click.

The original Chrome exercise needed a speech-service wakeup after tab switches:
a zero-volume empty utterance on `visibilitychange`. Retain and exercise that
workaround in the browser being used; it is a recorded compatibility behavior,
not a claim that every browser version fails identically.

### Pause

```
local_pause_cause = tts_queued_or_speaking OR user_typing
```

The Agent checks its gate before starting each tool; the server calls the
public Agent's `Pause` or `Unpause` on receiving those commands. Pause is
Agent-wide. An explicit unpause in any tab unpauses it for everyone; unchanged
local typing or speech in another tab cannot veto that decision. Rules:

1. TTS queues an utterance: send `pause`. Set the flag when the
   utterance is queued, not when audio begins.
2. TTS queue empties: send `unpause`, unless the user is typing.
3. User starts typing in the input: send `pause`, even with TTS off.
4. User sends (Enter): re-evaluate. Stay paused if TTS is speaking.
5. ESC with empty input: cancel TTS, re-evaluate.
6. Streaming into an already-running tool continues. Pause gates new
   starts only.
7. `onerror` on utterances must mirror `onend`. A Chrome `interrupted`
   error that does not continue the queue deadlocks it.
8. Edge-triggered: send pause/unpause on transitions, not on every
   utterance boundary.

### gui.log

The fourth log. Every WebSocket message in both directions,
timestamped. One line per message.

| log | captures | added in |
|---|---|---|
| event.log | agent events (append-only) | earlier chapters |
| api.log | LLM wire JSON | earlier chapters |
| debug.log | diagnostics | earlier chapters |
| **gui.log** | **WebSocket JSON, both directions** | **this chapter** |

### Yours

Markdown rendering library. ANSI-to-HTML approach. Visual styling.
TTS voice and speed. WebSocket library. Whether finalized Artifacts
replace or augment the streamed view. How the speaker icon looks.

### The exercise

Build an optional public-library GUI module: one Agent, one HTTP server on
`--port` (default 8088), serving its static files through `--gui-dir`. The
accepted example lives in `gui/`, with `cmd/` and `web/gui/` inside it; historical
chapter IDs in evidence remain `ch08`. The binary accepts prompts
over WebSocket, streams observations to all connected clients,
supports reconnection, gates tool calls on pause, and logs to gui.log.

Configuration uses public flags, including `--port`, `--gui-dir`, `--vendor`,
`--model`, `--base-url`, `--workspace`, `--event-log` and `--no-stream`.
Explicit flags override the inherited provider environment defaults. Keep
credentials in the intended process environment rather than command arguments.
The original flags-only sentence conflicted with its own environment-configured
grader; it did not justify breaking the earlier key setup.

```
go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 7 path/to/core
```

The grader builds the GUI module separately: `-gui DIR` selects it, defaulting
to `gui/` under the core. It builds `./cmd` when present, otherwise the module
root, and launches `--port` plus `--gui-dir` pointing to that module's `web/gui`.
HTTP `/` must become available and WebSocket `/ws` accepts the messages above.
Its faithful provider peer supplies the inherited `LLM_VENDOR`, `LLM_MODEL`,
`LLM_API_KEY` and `LLM_BASE_URL` environment. `-gui-model MODEL` selects the
declared Anthropic fixture row; the historical default `claude-sonnet-5` is a
local test-table entry, not a model-discovery claim. Earlier consumer, workflow,
media and streaming flags still apply to core parity.

The optional module must resolve its public core dependency to the submitted
core. This boundary check accompanies `websocket-streams`; source review still
establishes actual ownership and shared-Agent use. Active-partial replay,
handoff ordering, the fixed window, paused interrupt and browser behavior also
retain their source/integration checks. A WebSocket score alone cannot prove
what a card displays or what the listener hears.

| check | points | what it tests |
|---|---|---|
| `websocket-streams` | 25 | subscribe, prompt via WS; receive part_delta, part_final, state_changed, turn_ended, tool_dispatched, tool_finished with correct fields |
| `event-replay` | 20 | reconnect after a completed turn; recover the same final/tool content and artifact IDs, without stale partials |
| `gui-log` | 15 | gui.log contains timestamp, direction and JSON per line; both directions present |
| `pause-holds-tools` | 20 | between real tool calls, pause prevents the next start; explicit unpause from another tab releases it; all calls complete |
| `ch6-parity` | 20 | every Chapter 6 check still passes against the headless core |
| **total** | **100** | |

---

## 7.1 The idea in plain words

A radio station transmits regardless of how many receivers are tuned
in. Add a radio and it hears from that moment forward. Unplug one and
the station does not pause. Play the recording from an earlier
timestamp and hear what you missed.

The agent is the station. Observations are the broadcast: streaming
chunks, finalized parts, state changes, tool starts, tool completions.
The GUI is a radio. The event log is the recording; an observation buffer
alone would lose completed history when progress is dropped.

**The agent has no GUI code.** No WebSocket import, no rendering
dependency, no display flag in its configuration. The agent writes
observations through Ensemble's public seam from Chapter 5. An optional Go
WebSocket server subscribes there and projects history plus progress into
browser messages. Attach zero browsers and
the agent runs identically. Attach three and they all see the same
stream. Close a tab, reopen it an hour later, subscribe, and catch up from the event log in one burst.

**Everything is an Artifact.** Thinking text, chat text, tool call
arguments, tool results, user messages: they differ in how they look,
not in what they are. Each one streams in one of three formats
(markdown, ANSI, JSON), then optionally renders finalized HTML
specific to its type. One component, `ArtifactScroll`, manages the
scroll view. CSS classes make thinking dim and tool calls compact. The
renderer per type is a detail inside the component, not a separate
architecture.

**Pace is a safety mechanism, not a preference.** A human who cannot
watch the agent comfortably cannot steer it. The hint, the interrupt,
the decision to let a tool call proceed: all require seeing what the
agent is doing before it finishes doing it. TTS auto-speaks the stream
so the human hears without looking. Pause gates tool calls while the
human absorbs what just happened. The chapter after this one builds a
full three-pane workbench; this one builds the component it sits on.

---

## 7.2 Extending the broadcast

Chapter 5 built `PartDelta`, `PartFinal` and `StateChanged`;
Chapter 6 made the content incremental. They carry response content and
stored tool-result finals, but there is no explicit tool-start announcement.
The model requests a tool call; a display should be able to distinguish
execution starting from a result arriving later.

`ToolDispatched` fires before execution: call id, tool name, raw
input. `ToolFinished` carries the result of waiting: call id, result, error
flag. Chapter 4's distinction still holds. A timeout can return a handle while
the actual job continues, and its later output must remain visible even if
the human has interrupted the turn. `TurnEnded` announces the end of the turn
to displays; it does not replace the reliable completion used by `Ask`.

The names avoid a silent collision. The event log already has
`tool_called` and `tool_returned` for replay. The mailbox has its
internal worker reports to the actor. Three
systems, three names for what looks like the same thing: the event
is the record, the mailbox message is the signal, the observation
is the broadcast. Using the same name for two of them compiles fine
and produces a conversation about why something fired twice.

---

## 7.3 One tool at a time

The actor dispatches tools serially: start one, wait for its reported result,
start the next. A continuing job may outlive that wait. It has worked this
way since Chapter 5. What changes
is that the property now matters.

A pause gate that checks before each dispatch needs a gap between
dispatches in which to check. Parallel dispatch closes that gap:
three tools fire at once and a pause arriving a millisecond later has
nothing to stop. Serial dispatch creates the gap. The gate fills it.

The comment in the actor loop states the dependency rather than what
the code does:

```go
// Serial dispatch lets the pause gate hold execution between tools.
```

A comment that states *why* an architectural choice was made survives
the instinct to parallelize that hits every engineer who reads a
serial loop.

---

## 7.4 The pause gate

Pause is a live Agent control, not another conversation message waiting for
reduction. The Agent owns its gate. Common declares the public interface;
the behavior belongs with Agent, rather than in a shared utility package.
The GUI calls that Agent interface. It does not receive an Engine sibling,
become the Agent's parent, or create a second gate.

The accepted implementation uses a mutex and a wake channel. While paused,
a small boundary waiter waits for unpause or cancellation and reports back to
the actor. The actor keeps consuming its mailbox. Blocking that consumer would
strand exactly the interrupt the human is trying to send.

The wake reason is the design. Unpause permits the next dispatch; cancellation
ends the current turn. The Agent stays alive, another prompt can start, and
other jobs keep their real outcomes. Without context awareness, pause is a
trap: the human would have to remember to unpause before interrupting a turn,
under exactly the pressure where remembering extra steps fails.

The gate bypasses the mailbox deliberately. A mailbox message waits
in FIFO order behind pending tool completions, hints, and interrupts.
Pause is about the next dispatch boundary, and the Agent-owned gate has no
mailbox queue to wait in. A tool already admitted past that boundary continues;
pause is neither retroactive cancellation nor process shutdown.

---

## 7.5 The receiver

The hub implements the public identified observer. Its callback handles two
tiers: it captures new durable history and accumulates streaming content in an
in-flight map keyed by display identity. Live deltas send only the new chunk;
a reconnect receives the accumulated prefix. Then it returns. If a client's send
channel is full, the message is dropped for that client. The actor
does not wait for network I/O.

Each client has a write goroutine draining a buffered channel.
The observation callback iterates the set and does a non-blocking send on each.
The hub is a broadcaster: the station does not wait for the
radio.

Prompts and hints from the browser use the same public `Post` entrance as
terminal input. The actor classifies a busy user message as a hint; the browser
does not guess which turn should receive it. Blocking library callers still use
reliable request completion. Neither view runs another model loop.

The accepted composition root owns Agents, configuration stays with Agent,
and Engine reaches it through its actual parent. The transport owns sockets.
Public interfaces let it reach the existing Agent without making a socket
server a fictional parent or copying services into another bag.

Network sends and their trace writes happen in the connection's writer;
incoming messages are traced by its reader. Both stay outside the observation
callback. Disconnect uses a separate lifetime signal, and
shutdown joins writers before closing logs. A nonblocking send does not make
it safe to close a data channel another broadcaster can still reach.

---

## 7.6 The wire

The protocol has no sequence numbers and no cursor. A `subscribe`
message arrives empty. The server decides what history to send based on its
own fixed event-log window (last hour or last 100 renderable
events, whichever is larger), then sends any in-flight streaming
content, then switches to live delivery.

A reconnecting client and a fresh client use the same path. The
server does not need to know whether this is a first connection or a
tenth. The event-log window is the same either way. This is simpler
than tracking per-connection offsets, and better:
the client gets recent context whenever the Agent has any to give.

A subscription also receives current turn and pause state, marked as replay.
The turn snapshot uses the existing `state_changed` envelope with both `from`
and `to` equal to the current state. Equal endpoints report a snapshot without
inventing a transition. The student initially omitted `from`; that was a real
contract defect, not an optional-field convention. A fresh-subscription test
and a restored-defect mutation now check the complete envelope.

---

## 7.7 Two tiers of state

The hub holds two kinds of state, matching the two things a
connecting client needs.

**Tier 1: The event log.** Recorded facts from the append-only log:
finalized parts, tool calls and returns, user messages. On subscribe, the hub reads the recent
window and converts each event to a wire message the
client renders directly. They survive a browser disconnect while the Agent
continues. Restoring an Agent after a process restart belongs to the later
save/load chapter; writing a log does not implement restoration.

**Tier 2: In-flight partials.** Accumulated streaming content for
anything the agent is currently producing. A map from display identity to
the concatenated chunks received so far. On subscribe, the hub sends
the current partial for each active part. On `PartFinal`, the
partial is cleared. These are ephemeral: they exist only while
content is streaming.

Append-only is a history rule, not a synchronization primitive. Appending can
replace a Go slice's backing array while another goroutine reads it. The
history owner snapshots the requested suffix under its lock. The GUI then
coordinates that history frontier, its partial map and subscriber admission
under one handoff lock. A final cannot slip between a subscriber's completed
history and its old partial, leaving the same text on two cards.

The parser IDs from Chapter 6 are still local to one model response. The GUI
must retain cards across several responses and human turns. The actor assigns
an Agent-lifetime display ID to each part, uses it in root observations, and
stores it on the final part. Replay therefore names the same card that received
the live chunks. Provider call IDs and opaque signed content keep their original
meanings. A browser identity is not permission to rewrite provider history.

When a final is captured, remove its partial before publishing it. Sort active
partials by their assigned creation identities on replay; a Go map supplies no
stream order. On an interrupted turn, clear abandoned partials that will never
receive a final. Completed facts still come from history, including actual late
job output.

Replay and live progress need different admission rules. A live progress update
can be missed by a slow receiver, but silently dropping half its reconnect
history defeats the recovery path. The accepted server admits the whole replay
as one queued batch while adding the subscriber, then lets that connection's
writer send it outside the lock. A 270-event replay test exceeds the live queue's
256-batch capacity. A truncation mutant initially timed out without proving why;
after preserving terminal status, it failed directly at 249 versus 270 facts.

Another mutation removed final-part cleanup but passed: the test reconnected
after `TurnEnded`, which had already cleared every partial. Reconnecting while
tools were still running exposed the stale partial. The assertion had to observe
the interval in which the two cleanup paths differed.

For this chapter the window is fixed: include the last hour OR the last 100
renderable events, whichever reaches farther back. An event with several
rendered parts still counts as one event. A configurable policy is future work.

---

## 7.8 The fourth log

```
2026-09-17T14:32:01.123Z > {"type":"subscribe"}
2026-09-17T14:32:01.456Z < {"type":"part_delta","part_id":3,"kind":"text","chunk":"Hello"}
```

`>` is client-to-server. `<` is server-to-client. Each line has an RFC3339
timestamp, a direction marker and one compact JSON payload. The whole line
is not itself a JSON object. The optional transport owns this trace; general
diagnostics still belong to Ensemble's logger. This is
transport-layer tracing, the same tool as `api.log` for a different
wire.

A log missing one direction lies about what happened. The lie
surfaces at the worst moment: the message that was not delivered,
invisible in the record because the record only shows one side.

---

## 7.9 Everything is an Artifact

An Artifact streams, then finalizes. Thinking, chat, tool
arguments, tool results, user messages: all Artifacts. They differ
in CSS class and renderer, not in kind.

`ArtifactScroll` manages them. On `part_delta`: find or create by
part id, stream through the format renderer (markdown for thinking
and chat, JSON for tool arguments). On `part_final`: replace with
finalized HTML. On `tool_dispatched`: create a tool card. On
`tool_finished`: update it.

The alternative, ChatMessage plus ThinkingPanel plus ToolCallCard, encodes
assumptions about what the agent produces. An Artifact that knows
three rendering formats handles anything that fits one, which is
everything, because LLMs produce text in exactly the three varieties
the terminal already distinguished by colour.

Visual treatment comes from CSS classes: `artifact--thinking` gets
dim opacity, `artifact--tool` gets a compact layout. Adding a new treatment is a CSS rule.

The Go grader cannot establish safe DOM rendering or usable speech. Exercise
the actual page as well. An exercise whose output is invisible is an exercise
nobody finishes.

The student's live Gemini page revealed a less dramatic rendering error: a
legitimate empty text part displayed its own metadata. The renderer used a
truthiness test, then fell back to JSON. An empty string lost to the fallback.
The same shortcut would display opaque signatures and redacted thinking as if
they were words for the reader. Since the speaker button and automatic speech
used the card's text, the error crossed both channels.

The correction projects readable content explicitly. Empty text stays empty.
Readable Anthropic thinking and Gemini thought text can become prose; signature
and redacted bodies remain opaque replay material. Preserve those bytes in
history without pretending they are something to read aloud.

The focused browser test reused the retained Gemini part, plus readable and
opaque controls from an external peer. It checked the card, automatic speech
input and speaker-button input separately. Restoring the fallback failed all
three checks for each empty or opaque case, while readable controls still
produced native start/end events. No new model generation was needed to diagnose
what was already visible in the saved page.

---

## 7.10 The voice

TTS auto-speaks the stream. Thinking and chat in full. Tool
dispatches abbreviated: "read file: main.go, line 42." Tool results
silent. A speaker icon on every Artifact card speaks the accessible
text on click.

The original Chrome exercise found `speechSynthesis` asleep after a tab switch.
Its workaround sends a zero-volume empty utterance on `visibilitychange`.
Ugly, and worth recording where the next person building the queue can find it.
The accepted page keeps this wakeup outside the audible queue, so it does not
hold the pause gate.

`onerror` must mirror `onend`. Chrome fires `error` with reason
`interrupted` when one utterance cancels another, which is normal queue
behaviour. An error handler that does not advance the queue deadlocks
it: silence, permanent, no error message. Both callbacks mean "this
utterance is done, advance."

Queue phrases from the streamed text, not an utterance for every network chunk.
Keep unfinished phrases by artifact identity. A final flushes the remainder;
it must not read the whole answer again. Replayed history is silent until the
reader clicks its speaker. Keep a reference to the active utterance, and ignore
an old cancellation callback after a newer utterance has taken its place.

The native-browser test recorded a first utterance starting, a real
`speechSynthesis.cancel()` interruption, then the second utterance starting and
ending with pause released. A restored error-handler defect stranded the queue.
That proves the browser received and completed speech work. It does not prove
that a person heard an intelligible voice; listen as a separate part of using
the interface.

---

## 7.11 Pause in the browser

```
local_pause_cause = tts_queued_or_speaking OR user_typing
```

TTS queues an utterance: send `pause`. Queue empties: send `unpause`,
unless the input has text. User types: `pause`. User sends: stay
paused if TTS is speaking. ESC with empty input: cancel TTS,
re-evaluate.

Edge-triggered. Send `pause` on the transition, send `unpause` on
the reverse. The WebSocket carries transitions; the server holds state.
A client sending `pause` per queued utterance floods the wire with
messages that carry no information. More subtly, it can undo another tab's
explicit unpause. Local causes only send automatic commands when they change.
The **Unpause everyone** button releases the one Agent gate immediately.
An unchanged cause elsewhere cannot assert a veto, and reconnecting a tab
must not reassert its stale local pause state.

Streaming into a running tool continues. The gate is between tools,
not inside them.

---

## Taking it for a spin

Build from the optional GUI module's own directory:

```sh
go build -o /tmp/ch7gui ./cmd
```

Use the inherited provider setup: `LLM_VENDOR`, a discovered `LLM_MODEL`,
`LLM_API_KEY` in the intended child environment, and `LLM_BASE_URL` when an
endpoint override is needed. Flags override those defaults. Keep credentials
out of prompts, command arguments and logs. From a disposable working directory,
launch the binary with the actual absolute asset path:

```sh
/tmp/ch7gui --port 8088 --gui-dir /absolute/path/to/gui/web/gui
```

The working directory receives `event.log`, `api.log`, `debug.log` and
`gui.log`; the default tool workspace is that directory too. `--workspace`
can select another scratch project. The HTTP server listens on localhost and
serves the WebSocket at `/ws`. Its terminal remains another view of the same
Agent; terminal EOF detaches that input without shutting down the browser.

Open `http://localhost:8088`. Dark page, input field, "idle." Type a
prompt. Reasoning appears dim, the reply streams, TTS reads it. Ask
for a tool and a card appears with the arguments, the result fills
in, the reply continues.

Open a second tab. Both show the same stream. Close one, reopen:
it subscribes, receives the event-log window, catches up in a burst. Type a hint in the terminal; both tabs see
it. Start typing in the browser: "paused," no new tool starts.
Type `/interrupt` in the terminal: the current turn ends even while paused.
The Agent remains usable and running jobs continue. An explicit unpause from
the second tab must release the gate for both, even if the first tab still
contains unsent text.

Terminal and browser, two views of one agent, neither aware of the
other.

The retained October 9 exercise used installed Chrome and the real native
speech service. It checked two tabs, a connection during an active partial,
completed-history reload, safe markup, reachable long content, typing with
Read aloud off, another tab's unpause, speaker clicks, Escape and visibility
changes. [The browser receipt](../solutions/evidence/ch08/browser.json)
records 180 available voices and a short sentence's queued/start/end events.
That is an API observation, not a subjective listening result.

The speech check did not pass cleanly on the first try. Its first multi-tab
record contained a native `canceled` error. A later repeat waited for speech
that did not complete: reloading the second tab had restored its checked
Read aloud default, accidentally enabling overlapping speech during the long
response. Explicitly disabling that tab's voice after reload produced the
clean automatic-speech result. A separate
[interruption receipt](../solutions/evidence/ch08/speech.json)
checks that a real error advances the queue. Neither result justifies
inventing an audio-quality claim.

All three live provider turns ran an actual `run_command` and returned its
marker with exit code 0:

| Historical model used | Observed deltas | Actual tool marker |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `claude-sonnet-4-6` | 28 | `GUI_ANTHROPIC_OK` |
| `gpt-4o-mini` | 27 | `GUI_OPENAI_OK` |
| `gemini-3.8-flash` | 5 | `GUI_GEMINI_OK` |

The Anthropic run also carried a terminal busy hint into the browser on the
same Agent, and its speaker button produced native start/end events. The
Gemini run used Bill's required model and also exposed the empty-text metadata
card described above. Successful tool execution did not make the page correct.
The [live summary](../solutions/evidence/ch08/live-summary.json)
and [projection correction](../solutions/evidence/ch08/projection.json)
retain both the success and the subsequent repair. These are observed model
destinations, not a current availability list or a new paid run of this edition.

The original student GUI grader returned **55/100 FAIL** after roughly
47 minutes. It had built an earlier binary, before the replay-status fix:
the missing `from` field cost 25 points, while inherited CLI checks launched
the continuing GUI server and cost another 20. The original legacy solution
scored 100/100. Preserve those results rather than assigning a hypothetical
score to the corrected source. Final-source race tests, browser checks and
independent review established the bounded fixes. The revised grader now
uses the actual separate GUI and headless entry points; its detailed evidence
belongs in the [chapter review](../docs/edition-2-notes/enhancement-07-code.md).

---

## What Chapter 8 does with this

One scroll pane, one input field, one dark page. Chapter 8 adds the
workspace: a second `ArtifactScroll` for tool calls and results, an
agent tree, drag bars, settings, and a sidebar that grows as chapters
add features. The Artifact is the reusable unit. The layout is what
remains.

---

# Chapter 8: Build Your Dream GUI

Get ready for self-wielding. This is the ignition chapter, where you
can finally start using your AI coding agent to write itself. At the
end of this chapter your agent will not compete with Claude Code, and
that is fine. What matters is making the switch as soon as you can be
productive with the new system, because living inside your own agent
is how you discover the bugs and the missing features. This chapter gives you the
freedom to create whatever GUI makes sense to you.

In my case, text-to-speech is critical, and you will find it built
into the reference solution. We are wandering into territory where
the grader cannot help. This is an AI coding agent for you, not for
the LLM, so you will have to drive. Later GUI-driving work can give
control back to the LLM so it can test the system end-to-end, but
for now, you are the one in control.

Chapter 7 gave you one scroll pane on a dark page. It works. You can
watch the agent think, see tool calls arrive, pause to read. As a
safety floor it is complete: a human can watch, and that is the
threshold that matters.

Nobody customizes a safety floor, checks whether their preferences
survived a restart, or drags a divider to put chat on one side and
tool calls on the other, unless the tool they are watching is one
they intend to use every day. This chapter
crosses that line. By the end, the page has three panes, a settings
panel that persists through the same WebSocket, theming that redraws
in fifteen CSS variables, and a sidebar with an agent tree that
currently shows exactly one node. The graded surface is small: four
server-side settings checks and a parity gate. Everything else is
client code you can see working.

## TL;DR

The optional GUI server gains a small settings store: a mutex, a value, a file
path. Browser preferences and their persistence belong in that module. The
Agent owns its effective `max_tool_rounds`; the saved envelope restores that
existing runtime policy through the public Agent interface.
Clients send `update_settings` over the WebSocket. The hub applies the
change, persists it, and broadcasts `settings_changed` to every
connected client. A new client receives `current_settings` on
subscribe.

The client gains a three-pane layout (sidebar, chat, actions), two
drag bars, theming via CSS custom properties, a settings panel, and an
agent tree with one node.

From the repository root, grade the core and its optional GUI separately:

```sh
go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 8 path/to/core
```

`-gui DIR` selects the GUI module, defaulting to `gui/` under the core.
Its existing `--port` and `--gui-dir` launch, provider environment defaults,
public dependency boundary and `-gui-model` fixture selection carry forward
from Chapter 7; earlier parity flags remain available. No model call is needed to
echo a preference. The restart check launches a new process in the same
disposable working directory, rather than asking the old process for its state.

| check | pts | what it tests |
|---|---|---|
| settings-roundtrip | 25 | `update_settings` → `settings_changed` with matching values |
| settings-on-connect | 20 | `current_settings` sent on subscribe |
| settings-broadcast | 20 | second client receives `settings_changed` |
| settings-persist | 15 | settings survive server restart |
| ch7-parity | 20 | every Chapter 7 check still passes against the appropriate core and GUI clients |

The settings fixture starts with light theme, TTS true, speed 1.5 and font 18;
it then patches dark theme/speed 2, false TTS/budget 2, budget 0, and system
theme. Each full echo and other-client snapshot must preserve the known fields.
Fresh subscription and process restart must return system, false, 2, 18 and 0.
These are test inputs, not mandated defaults or UI range endpoints. Runtime
budget enforcement, invalid-load handling, failed writes and actual browser
controls still require their source/integration evidence.

The original four checks cover the server, not the client-side layout,
theming, tree or native speech. Drive the actual browser and inspect the
effective values. Seeing a saved label is not enough, as the speech-rate
correction below demonstrates.

Four obligations survive the absence of a grader. The first three shipped
broken in the first edition's reference implementation and stayed broken
until its Chapter 13 drove the GUI with a second agent. The fourth survived
until the single-loop retirement audit.

**Validate where the value enters.** A settings field arriving over the
wire is untrusted input. Clamp it in the apply path and again on the
load-from-disk path, rather than at the point of use. The first edition's
audit recorded a temperature of -5 reaching the engine because both paths
trusted the sender. Apply the same lesson to this chapter's actual fields;
that historical example does not add a temperature setting here.

**Decide whether a settings message is a patch or a snapshot.** The two
need different handling of absence. A sparse patch changes only fields that
are present; an explicit zero or false is still a change. `omitempty` on an
ordinary Go boolean cannot express both "absent" and "set false". Decode a
sparse object over a copy of the accepted value, or represent presence
explicitly. A full snapshot must include zero and false. Dropping a clamped
zero from the broadcast leaves the client displaying the number the server
already rejected; dropping false prevents the server from turning TTS off.

**Put control state in an attribute, not a CSS class.** A class styles a
toggle and tells a screen reader nothing, and an automated observer
reads the same nothing.

**Prove that a setting changes behavior.** Persistence and broadcast can
both work while the execution path ignores the value. `max_tool_rounds`
did exactly that: two orchestration loops read a hard-coded limit of 16
while the GUI faithfully saved 200. Chapter 5 now has one owner and one
policy: zero selects the named default of 200; positive N permits N tool
batches per human turn. Read the setting at turn start so an update takes
effect on the next turn, not halfway through the current one. Test both a
small saved limit that stops execution and a large one that permits more
than 16 batches, through the actual entry point and across a restart.

The four visible controls remain theme, TTS enabled, speech speed and font
size. `max_tool_rounds` already belongs to the execution exercise; it travels
in the settings envelope without requiring another GUI control. Reject
negative budgets at the public Agent boundary; the GUI's shared validation
path may clamp them to zero before calling it. Keep those two boundaries
distinct rather than teaching the Engine to repair browser preferences.

## The Why

An agent without preferences is a tool you configure by editing
source. An agent whose preferences vanish on restart is one that
wastes the first thirty seconds of every session re-learning what you
told it. The smallest useful settings system is: accept a change over
the wire, write it to disk, tell every watcher, read it back on
startup. That is four operations, and the grader tests each one.

The layout and theming are the other half. They are not graded because
"does it look right" is a human judgment, and you are the human. The
grader trusts you to open a browser.

## Three panes and a drag bar

The layout is three columns: a left sidebar, a center pane for chat,
and a right pane for tool output. Two vertical drag bars separate
them.

```css
.layout {
  display: flex;
  height: 100vh;
  overflow: hidden;
}
.sidebar    { width: 260px; min-width: 180px; }
.drag-bar   { width: 6px; cursor: col-resize; background: var(--border); }
.center     { flex: 1; min-width: 300px; }
.actions    { width: 380px; min-width: 200px; }
```

A drag bar is three events:

```javascript
bar.addEventListener('mousedown', e => {
  const startX = e.clientX;
  const startW = left.offsetWidth;
  const move = e2 => {
    left.style.width = Math.max(180, startW + e2.clientX - startX) + 'px';
  };
  const up = () => {
    document.removeEventListener('mousemove', move);
    document.removeEventListener('mouseup', up);
  };
  document.addEventListener('mousemove', move);
  document.addEventListener('mouseup', up);
});
```

No library, and the minimum-width clamp is already in
the `Math.max` call. If you want the right pane to resize too, copy
the same handler with a sign flip on the delta.

The accepted page uses pointer capture so dragging beyond a six-pixel divider
does not lose the gesture. Focused dividers also accept arrow keys and expose
their value as a separator attribute. These are small controls over the same
width change; they do not need another layout system.

## Routing artifacts to the right pane

Chapter 7 built `ArtifactScroll`. This chapter uses it twice.

```javascript
const chatScroll    = new ArtifactScroll(centerEl);
const actionsScroll = new ArtifactScroll(actionsEl);
```

The WebSocket message handler routes by type:

```javascript
function handleMessage(msg) {
  const tool = msg.type === 'tool_dispatched' ||
    msg.type === 'tool_finished' || msg.kind === 'tool_call' ||
    msg.part?.type === 'tool_call';
  (tool ? actionsScroll : chatScroll).receive(msg);
}
```

Text/thinking deltas and finals, and `user_message`, go to chat. Tool-call
argument deltas and finals go to actions, along with `tool_dispatched` and
`tool_finished`. Preserve their artifact and call identities so dispatch
updates the card that already showed the parameters. Status messages update
the workbench's state controls. The routing is a filter, not a fork: both panes use the same
ArtifactScroll API, the same CSS, the same streaming protocol. The
abstraction that Chapter 7 promised holds up under reuse. If it had
not, you would know it here, because the right pane would need its own
rendering logic.

## Settings over the wire

The server needs four things: a place to put settings, a way to
change them, a way to notify, and a way to persist.

```go
// Settings is a complete snapshot; false and zero must stay on the wire.
type Settings struct {
    // Theme follows dark, light or the browser's system preference.
    Theme      string  `json:"theme"`
    // TTSEnabled controls automatic speech.
    TTSEnabled bool    `json:"tts_enabled"`
    // TTSSpeed is the rate consumed by the next native utterance.
    TTSSpeed   float64 `json:"tts_speed"`
    // FontSize is the interface text size in pixels.
    FontSize   int     `json:"font_size"`
    // MaxToolRounds saves the Agent's next-turn policy; zero selects 200.
    MaxToolRounds int  `json:"max_tool_rounds"`
}
```

Keep this value in the optional GUI server, under its existing mutex. The
student first put browser settings and their file handling in the core Agent;
review of the ownership boundary moved them back out. Agent-owned configuration
does not make a theme or a slider a core concern. Only the effective tool budget
belongs to the Agent, and snapshots read it from that owner.

The original `ApplyRaw` sketch ignored decoding and write errors while mutating
the live state. Decode a sparse object onto a copy instead. This excerpt uses
the accepted example's local ranges; those endpoints are implementation choices,
not additional exercise requirements:

```go
func settingsPatch(current Settings, raw json.RawMessage) (Settings, error) {
    raw = bytes.TrimSpace(raw)
    if len(raw) == 0 || raw[0] != '{' {
        return current, fmt.Errorf("settings must be a JSON object")
    }
    next := current
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &next); err != nil {
        return current, fmt.Errorf("invalid settings: %w", err)
    }
    switch next.Theme {
    case "dark", "light", "system":
    default:
        next.Theme = "dark"
    }
    next.TTSSpeed = max(0.5, min(2, next.TTSSpeed))
    next.FontSize = max(12, min(24, next.FontSize))
    next.MaxToolRounds = max(0, next.MaxToolRounds)
    return next, nil
}
```

The same helper validates disk input. A missing file starts with defaults;
malformed saved JSON reports a startup error rather than silently throwing away
preferences. A type error halfway through a patch cannot leave half an update
in the accepted value.

Persist the candidate before publishing it. The accepted server writes a small
replacement file and renames it over the destination; if either operation fails,
the previous accepted value stays active and no success snapshot is broadcast.
This is error handling for one settings file, not a transaction framework or a
claim of power-loss durability. The existing server mutex orders apply,
persistence, publication and new subscriptions.

The WebSocket request carries only the changed fields:

```json
{"type":"update_settings","settings":{"tts_enabled":false,"max_tool_rounds":0}}
```

After a successful save, update the Agent's effective budget through its public
setter, then send `settings_changed` with the full settings
object to every connected client. The sender receives it too, which
confirms the round trip. A new subscriber receives `current_settings`
during the subscribe handshake alongside history and current partials; no new
`event_range` envelope is required. For example, after the other settings have
been set to system theme, speed 2 and font size 18, the snapshot includes:

```json
{"type":"settings_changed","settings":{"theme":"system","tts_enabled":false,"tts_speed":2,"font_size":18,"max_tool_rounds":0}}
```

If decoding or writing fails, report the error instead of broadcasting success.
The accepted page displays the existing `settings_error` reply. Test with an
actual filesystem failure as well as malformed JSON; a happy round trip never
exercises the publication order. The file path is chosen at the application
boundary: the accepted command uses `cr/settings.json` under its working
directory. Restarting that command restores preferences and the next-turn
budget, not a saved conversation.

No REST endpoint. No `/api/settings`. The WebSocket already carries
observations, partial text, state changes, and event-log replays. One
more message type uses the existing ordering. A second transport would add
two sources of truth, and they will disagree the moment a tab
hibernates.

The saved budget needs a test that reaches execution. The accepted entry-point
test builds the actual two-view application, saves a two-batch limit, and
restarts it. While the first provider response is held, a settings update changes
the saved limit to eighteen. The active turn still stops after two batches;
the next terminal turn completes eighteen. Another restart retains eighteen,
and zero again permits more than sixteen by selecting the existing default 200.
Only the external provider is fake; the actor, tools, stdin, WebSocket and file
all remain real.

Reading live configuration on every tool dispatch would look more responsive
and be wrong. Restoring that defect made the active turn run eighteen batches
when it should have stopped at two. A setting can change immediately in the
panel while its documented execution policy starts with the next turn.

## Theming

Fifteen CSS custom properties redraw the entire page:

```css
:root, [data-theme="dark"] {
  --bg: #0d0d0d;
  --fg: #e0e0e0;
  --surface: #1a1a1a;
  --border: #333;
  --accent: #5b9bd5;
  --accent-hover: #7ab3e8;
  --thinking-bg: #1a1a2e;
  --code-bg: #1e1e1e;
  --input-bg: #1a1a1a;
  --input-border: #444;
  --sidebar-bg: #111;
  --drag-bar: #333;
  --tool-bg: #1a1a1a;
  --error-bg: #2d1a1a;
  --scrollbar-thumb: #444;
}
```

Dark is the default because this agent was built for a user who reads
by speech and does not need brightness. Every element uses `var(--bg)`
instead of `#0d0d0d`, so adding a light theme is writing fifteen new
values:

```css
[data-theme="light"] {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --fg: #1a1a1a;
  --surface: #f5f5f5;
  /* ... */
}
```

`document.body.dataset.theme = settings.theme` applies a concrete theme. One
assignment, no class toggling, no re-render. A `system` option first resolves
`prefers-color-scheme`:

```javascript
if (theme === 'system') {
  const dark = matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches;
  document.body.dataset.theme = dark ? 'dark' : 'light';
}
```

Also listen for the media query's `change` event while system theme is selected.
A one-time lookup makes the page follow the operating system only until the
operating system changes its mind.

## The agent tree

The sidebar shows one node: the agent's name and its state.

```html
<ul class="agent-tree">
  <li class="agent-node" data-state="idle">
    <span class="agent-indicator"></span>
    <span class="agent-name">Ensemble</span>
  </li>
</ul>
```

The indicator pulses in the accent colour when the agent is working, dims when idle.
`state_changed` messages update `data-state`, and CSS does the rest:

```css
.agent-indicator {
  width: 8px; height: 8px;
  border-radius: 50%;
  background: var(--accent);
  opacity: 0.3;
}
[data-state="in_flight"] .agent-indicator,
[data-state="tools_pending"] .agent-indicator {
  opacity: 1;
  animation: pulse 1.5s ease-in-out infinite;
}
```

Those names must match the Agent's actual state vocabulary. The student copied
the original example's `thinking` and `tool_use` into both the CSS and its first
browser check. The reducer emitted `in_flight` and `tools_pending`; the indicator
did not pulse. The corrected check inspects the active node's computed animation,
not just an attribute the test and CSS agreed to invent. Restoring the old
selectors makes it fail.

The data model is a tree:

```javascript
agents = [{
  id: 'root',
  name: 'Ensemble',
  state: 'idle',
  children: []
}];
```

The `children` array stays empty in this exercise. The rendering code walks
the tree recursively, but there is still only one Agent. The display model
does not create children, define their lifetimes or invent a sub-agent protocol.

## Sidebar tabs

The left sidebar cycles between two tabs: **Agents** and
**Settings**. The settings panel contains:

- Theme selector (dark, light, system)
- TTS toggle
- TTS speed slider
- Font size selector

Each control sends `update_settings` with the changed field. The
server echoes `settings_changed`. The handler applies it locally:

```javascript
ws.addEventListener('message', e => {
  const msg = JSON.parse(e.data);
  if (msg.type === 'settings_changed' || msg.type === 'current_settings') {
    applySettings(msg.settings);
  }
});
```

`applySettings` sets the theme, updates TTS and adjusts font size from the
accepted snapshot. Handle the initial snapshot as well as later changes.
Disabling speech cancels the local queue; a changed speech rate applies to
the next utterance. A successful update reaches the sender and other connected
clients; a fresh subscription or restart restores that saved state. Existing
slow-client progress limits still apply, so this is not a new reliable-message
transport.

### The saved number that speech never used

The settings server accepted and saved speed **1.75**. The label displayed
**1.75** after restart. Native speech ran at approximately **1.8**.

The independent reviewer followed the number past the WebSocket echo. The
range input had `step="0.1"`, so Chrome sanitized its value to 1.8. The label
read the saved object; the speech queue read the slider. Both halves behaved
as written, and they disagreed about what the person had selected.

The correction was one attribute, with a reason beside it:

```html
<!-- Saved rates may fall between tenths; preserve them in the slider. -->
<input id="tts-speed" type="range" min="0.5" max="2" step="any" value="1" />
```

Those bounds are the accepted example's choice. The important relationship is
that the server's accepted values survive the control and reach the consumer.
The focused check saved 1.75, restarted the real application, inspected the
snapshot, label and slider, then submitted browser input and recorded the
native utterance's rate. It repeated with **1.2345**, so a smaller fixed step
could not merely move the defect.

| Saved value | Correct slider and label | Correct native rate | Native rate with step 0.1 restored |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1.75 | 1.75 | 1.75 | 1.7999999523162842 |
| 1.2345 | 1.2345 | 1.2345000505447388 | 1.2000000476837158 |

Both correct and defective utterances produced native start/end events.
Completion did not establish that the requested speed was used. The
[baseline](../solutions/evidence/ch09/speed-r1.json) and
[restored defect](../solutions/evidence/ch09/speed-r1-mutation.json)
capture the values before asserting, so a failing check does not erase the
wrong rate it was meant to observe.

This was separate from an earlier test precision mistake. A saved 0.6 reached
the native API as `0.6000000238418579`; an exact equality check timed out.
The focused regression uses a tolerance of 0.00001, small enough for that
representation noise and much smaller than the 1.75-to-1.8 error. An earlier
timeout lacked enough retained location detail to assign it the same cause.
Keep the failed attempts without turning every test failure into a product bug.

Native callbacks and measured rates establish API behavior. They do not claim
that a person listened or found the speech intelligible. That still belongs
to driving the interface described in the opener.

## Taking it for a spin

Build and launch the optional GUI module as in Chapter 7, using a scratch
working directory and its absolute `web/gui` path. Keep the same working
directory when restarting to test `cr/settings.json`; a fresh empty directory
would test defaults instead. Provider credentials remain in the intended child
environment, outside preferences, commands, logs and browser controls.

Open two tabs. Change theme, turn Read aloud off and change font size in one;
the other should show the accepted values. Select system theme and change the
browser's OS preference. Drag each divider, focus it and try the arrow keys.
Start a tool turn: the one tree node should pulse, arguments and output should
appear in Actions, and the reply should remain in Chat. Restart the process
and check the visible controls, then the actual next utterance's rate.

The retained headed-Chrome exercise passed twelve checks covering those
client behaviors, including both pointer dividers and visible restoration of
all four preferences. Its final generic speed-control check uses the native
End key and rate 2; the separate fractional-rate test supplies the coverage
that the earlier tenths-aligned input missed. The
[browser receipt](../solutions/evidence/ch09/browser-r1.json)
records the checks and actual native callbacks.

A bounded live `gpt-4o-mini` turn followed model discovery. The browser saved
light theme, font 18 and TTS off, then restored them after restart. The model
ran a shell command whose actual output was `CH09_LIVE_OK`, with exit code 0;
Actions showed that result and Chat showed the answer. A terminal hint to keep
the reply to one sentence appeared on the same Agent. Clicking the answer's
speaker produced native start/end events. The
[live receipt](../solutions/evidence/ch09/live.json) preserves that
interaction. Unchanged Anthropic and required Gemini 3.8 coverage reuses the
preceding chapter's runs; settings did not justify another paid provider matrix.

The original student grader returned **80/100 FAIL**: all four new settings
checks passed, inherited parity did not. Its roughly 47-minute duration was
estimated from the output file's timestamps while the nested CLI checks ran
against the continuing GUI server. The original legacy solution scored
100/100. Neither score tested the speech-rate defect. Preserve the actual
earlier-build result and the later browser correction separately; the revised
grader uses the appropriate GUI and core entry points. The
[grader review](../docs/edition-2-notes/enhancement-08-code.md) records its
new results and their limits.

## What is not graded and why

The layout, the drag bars, the theming, the agent tree, the sidebar
tabs, the TTS controls. All client-side JavaScript and CSS. The grader
runs Go and connects via WebSocket. It can verify that
`update_settings` echoes correctly, that a second client sees the
change, that a restart preserves the file. It cannot verify that the
center pane is wider than 300 pixels or that the drag bar feels
smooth.

The grader covers its chosen machine checks; actual browser tests can also
measure layout and control behavior. The student supplies the judgment about
comfort, visibility and listening. Both are
necessary, and pretending one replaces the other is how codebases end
up with a green dashboard and a broken product.

## Making the switch

One working Agent, two artifact panes, preferences that survive a restart.
The value of this workbench is that someone can live in it long enough to
discover what the next improvement should be. A tree that can draw one node
does not establish sub-agent execution, and this chapter adds neither model
selection nor API-key controls. The original next-chapter forecast ran ahead
of the available exercise; it is not a requirement to invent those features.

Bill's destination for the new Ensemble is explicit: run GPT-6 Astra at high
reasoning, then use that Ensemble agent to build Edition 3 instead of Codex.
A usable workbench is progress toward that destination. Model access, the
reasoning setting and real coding use still need their own verification before
claiming the crossover. Starting useful work early, as the opener urges, is
how the remaining gaps become visible.

# Chapter 9: Skills

Every chapter so far has added capability by adding code. That stops
scaling. The agent already has file tools, process tools and job controls,
and the system prompt can grow with every feature. A configurable primary
skill was deliberately deferred until now. The system prompt is an easily abused
feature in LLM applications: teams stuff instructions, context, tool
descriptions, and user preferences into a monolith whose supposedly stable
prefix changes on every edit. Skills fix this before the problem arrives.

A skill is a named unit of capability: instructions, tools, and
dependencies, in a single markdown file. Loading one changes what the
agent can do; unloading one marks it for removal at the next
compaction. This chapter records that pending state; compaction arrives later.
The system prompt renders once from the primary skill at
agent creation and stays fixed. Capabilities added after creation
reach the agent through the event stream.

Variable substitution lives here too. A skill body can contain
`$TOOLS` or `$SKILLS` or any application-specific variable, and the
renderer replaces them at the point of use. The initial system prompt
gets creation-time values; a dynamically loaded skill gets the values
current at load time.

## TL;DR

Extend Chapter 8 with a per-Agent skills registry. A SKILL.md file lives in
a named directory under the skills root:

```
skills/
  base/
    SKILL.md
  code-tools/
    SKILL.md
  search-tools/
    SKILL.md
  read-tools/
    SKILL.md
  refactor-tools/
    SKILL.md
```

Each SKILL.md has flat YAML-style frontmatter between `---` markers and a
markdown body. This example requires the named dependency and offered skill
to have their own files:

```yaml
---
name: code-tools
description: File editing and search tools
type: loadable
tools: edit_file write_file search_files
depends: read-tools
loadable-skills: refactor-tools
---

You now have access to file editing tools.

Available tools: $TOOLS
Available skills to load: $SKILLS
```

**Frontmatter fields:**

- `name`: skill identifier
- `description`: one-line summary
- `type`: `primary` (agent identity, loaded at creation), `loadable`
  (offered to the agent, loaded on demand), or `dependency` (pulled
  in automatically, hidden)
- `tools`: tools this skill enables (FlexibleList: space-separated
  or YAML list)
- `depends`: skills to auto-load when this skill loads
- `loadable-skills`: skills this skill makes available for the agent
  to discover

The primary skill defines the agent. Its body, together with its initial
dependencies' instructions, becomes the system prompt, rendered once at
creation. Its `tools` list and those dependencies determine startup capability;
`load_skill` and `unload_skill` are always available when skills are configured.
A minimal `base` skill can declare only `read_file`. A full `ensemble` skill
declares the tools built so far:

```yaml
---
name: ensemble
description: Full AI coding agent
type: primary
tools:
  - read_file
  - write_file
  - edit_file
  - list_directory
  - search_files
  - run_command
  - wait_for_job
  - send_input
  - kill_job
  - tool_limits
  - load_skill
  - unload_skill
loadable-skills: code-tools search-tools
---
You are an autonomous AI coding agent.

## Available Tools

$TOOLS

## Available Skills

$SKILLS
```

The original example named `think` without teaching its behavior or arguments.
An unknown name cannot create a handler. This list uses the existing
`tool_limits` capability instead; do not advertise a tool that cannot execute.

The exercise is:

1. Discover the files and validate each skill's name and type. Accept both
   list forms shown below and preserve horizontal rules in the body.
2. Load the selected primary and its dependencies at Agent creation. Render
   the system text once; later skill loads leave it byte-for-byte unchanged.
3. Implement `load_skill` and `unload_skill`, each taking a JSON object such
   as `{"name":"code-tools"}`. A successful load resolves dependencies,
   enables tools, reveals the next available skills and returns rendered
   instructions through the existing tool result. Reject unavailable names,
   wrong types, missing dependencies and cycles without a partial activation.
4. Use the same enabled set for vendor declarations and dispatch. A guessed
   hidden name must not execute. Mark unload pending while retaining its
   instructions and tools; actual removal waits for the later compaction chapter.
5. Support `$TOOLS`, `$SKILLS` and application variables at point of use.
   Track each tool's first enabling source and event sequence. Keep registries
   independent between Agents and preserve earlier behavior without a skill spec.

From the core module, build the headless command. With ordinary provider
settings already configured, the public launch is:

```sh
go build -o /tmp/ensemble-ch09 .
EN_SKILLS_DIR=path/to/skills EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=base /tmp/ensemble-ch09 prompt "load the code-tools skill"
```

Use `chat` in place of `prompt TEXT` for the human interface. Both CLI and
optional GUI translate the same skill environment values into per-Agent
construction inputs. The GUI keeps Chapter 7's separate module and launch.
`EN_CUSTOM_VAR` supplies `$CUSTOM_VAR` for these commands; it is an application
example rather than a reason for the registry to read process environment.

From the repository root, grade the submitted core and its optional GUI:

```sh
go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 9 path/to/core
```

`-gui DIR` selects the GUI module, defaulting to `gui/` under the core;
`-gui-model` and inherited consumer, workflow, media and streaming fixture
options remain available. The skills phases use the actual WebSocket prompt
path. Headless parity uses the headless command.

| Check | Points | Observable behavior |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Initial tools | 10 | Primary/dependency tools plus both lifecycle tools |
| Primary body | 10 | Rendered initial instructions stay fixed across loads |
| Full primary | 10 | All twelve installed tools in the example are declared |
| Dynamic tools | 15 | Load adds instructions and executable tools; pending unload retains capability |
| Progressive disclosure | 15 | A load reveals its offered skills in current `$SKILLS` |
| Dependencies | 10 | Dependencies contribute both tools and instructions |
| Variables | 10 | Placeholder values reflect their rendering time |
| Unavailable skill | 5 | An unreachable skill is refused |
| Chapter 8 parity | 15 | Prior checks still pass through their appropriate clients |

The numeric checks do not prove every obligation. Dependency cycles, failed-load
atomicity, provenance and Agent isolation also need focused source tests and
review. Exercise the real registry and tool loop, replacing only the external
provider with a small fake where deterministic replies are needed.

## The Format

The parser splits the file on `---` with a limit of 3, protecting
against horizontal rules in the body. Frontmatter is key-value,
one field per line. Multi-value fields use FlexibleList. Both
formats parse to `[]string`:

```yaml
# Space-separated on one line
tools: edit_file write_file search_files

# YAML list
tools:
  - edit_file
  - write_file
  - search_files
```

The supported format is deliberately small: scalar fields and these two list
forms. There is no need for a general YAML document processor. Require the
opening frontmatter boundary, a name and one of the three types; report a
malformed file with its path. The directory locates the file, while `name`
identifies the skill in `depends` and tool arguments. Reject duplicate names
rather than letting directory order choose an identity.

Three skill types control visibility. A `primary` skill loads at
agent creation and defines the agent's identity. An offered `loadable` skill
appears in the available-skills list. The initial list is rendered into the
system prompt; later lists arrive with loaded instructions. The agent
calls `load_skill` to activate it. A `dependency` skill is invisible
to the agent; it loads automatically when a skill that depends on it
loads.

## The Registry

`SkillRegistry` discovers skills from a directory (one subdirectory
per skill) and tracks their state through a lifecycle. The name describes a
responsibility; it need not be an exported concrete type:

```
Discovered → LoadInitial (at creation)
           → LoadDynamic (by load_skill tool)
           → PendingUnload (by unload_skill; removal is a later chapter)
```

Loading resolves dependencies recursively. If `search-tools` depends
on `search-helpers`, both load and both contribute their tools. Cycle
detection uses a visiting set. A depends B depends A produces an
error, not infinite recursion.

Resolve the whole graph before enabling any of it. If the first dependency
supplies `write_file` and the second is missing, an error accompanied by a newly
enabled writer is a partial success the caller never asked for. A visiting set
and a resolved order let the registry validate first, then activate dependencies
before the requested skill. Their instructions travel with their tools.

Discovery reads definitions; it grants no capability. The registry belongs to
one Agent even when several Agents read the same directory. Its required parent
is that Agent, supplied through the common interface; the composition root
attaches both sides before loading the primary. Keep parsing, traversal and
rendering in the skills package. Shared types and interfaces remain in common.

The command's environment variables are construction convenience. An embedding
application passes its skills directory and primary choice to the Agent it is
creating. Changing a process-wide primary must not change every live Agent's
identity. Omitting the optional skill specification preserves the earlier
public tool-registration path.

The registry answers two questions the agent asks constantly: "what
tools can I use?" and "what skills can I load
next?" (`LoadableSkills`). The loadable set is the union of all
loaded skills' `loadable-skills` lists, restricted to discovered `loadable`
skills and minus anything already loaded. A dependency does not become directly
loadable merely because someone puts its name in that list.

The enabled-tool answer must reach execution as well as the request renderer.
Hiding `write_file` from the declaration array still leaves a working writer if
dispatch consults only the installed-handler table. Test the guessed name before
loading its skill: it should return an ordinary tool error and leave the file
absent. Then load the skill and prove that the same real handler can write it.
This checks both sides of the boundary without replacing the tool with a mock.

`unload_skill` marks a loaded name pending and reports that fact. It does not
rewrite old instructions or disable the skill's tools in this exercise. An
unloaded name returns an error. Compaction later provides the boundary where
removal becomes effective; adding a compactor now would turn a lifecycle marker
into another assignment.

## Progressive Disclosure

Loading a skill reveals more skills. The `$SKILLS` variable updates
to show what the agent can load next: `code-tools` might reveal
`refactor-tools`, which in turn reveals `architecture-tools`. The
tree unfolds as the agent explores.

The agent sees only one level ahead: the skills made available by
the ones already loaded. Context stays focused and the tool list
stays manageable.

The original `$SKILLS` text in the system prompt does not change as this tree
unfolds. The newly loaded body's `$SKILLS` is rendered after activation and
arrives in the tool result, where it can name the next level. This is how the
agent discovers `refactor-tools` without rebuilding its initial instructions.

## Variable Substitution

Skill bodies contain `$VAR` placeholders. A small map of names to renderer
functions is enough. The skills package supplies `$TOOLS` and `$SKILLS` from
the owning Agent's enabled declarations and current loadable set. Application
variables enter through the public API. For example, given the existing
Ensemble root `app` and its provider configuration `cfg`:

```go
agent, err := app.NewAgent(cfg, ensemble.AgentSpec{
    SkillsDir: "skills",
    PrimarySkill: "base",
    Variables: map[string]func() string{
        "CUSTOM_VAR": func() string { return "creation value" },
    },
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}
// Future loads see the new renderer; the primary text is already frozen.
agent.RegisterVar("CUSTOM_VAR", func() string { return "load-time value" })
```

The constructor's variables must be installed before primary rendering.
`RegisterVar` changes future renderings. It cannot reach back into text already
sent to a model. Select non-secret settings or context deliberately; substituting
a value puts it into model-visible instructions, so an environment variable
holding a credential is not a suitable example.

Variables render at point of use: the initial system prompt gets
creation-time lists, and a skill loaded mid-conversation gets
whatever the lists contain at load time.

In the accepted implementation, unknown placeholders remain visible verbatim.
A missing `$CUSTOM_VAR` is easier to diagnose that way than as a silently empty
sentence. Render callbacks outside the registry lock: `$TOOLS` reads declarations,
which consult the same enabled-tool state. Holding the lock while calling it
would deadlock the first useful variable.

## Tool Provenance

Every tool in the registry tracks its source:

```go
// ToolMeta records when this Agent first gained a tool.
type ToolMeta struct {
    // Source distinguishes creation-time and later capabilities.
    Source ToolSource
    // EventSeq is zero for initial tools, otherwise the enabling tool_called.
    EventSeq uint64
}
```

If the primary already enabled `read_file`, loading another skill that also
names it must preserve its initial provenance. A newly enabled `write_file`
records the sequence of the actual `load_skill` call that enabled it. Use the
existing event identity rather than inventing a separate skill counter.

Most renderers ignore this metadata at this stage. It gives a later renderer
enough information to distinguish initial declarations from dynamic additions
without knowing about skills. That matters when arranging a stable request
prefix for caching. The metadata alone does not preserve a cache hit: this
chapter still changes the tool declarations, and provider-specific placement,
cache markers and measured grants belong to the caching work later in the book.

## The Constitution

When `load_skill` runs, the skill's instructions arrive as the tool
result. They flow through the message history, not the system prompt.
Capabilities grow while the system prompt stays frozen at its
creation-time content.

That separation matters for memory. Pre-loaded context (memories,
user preferences, project notes) belongs in the message history as
data rather than the system prompt as instructions. The system prompt stays
separate from those changing facts. Chapter 22 builds the memory cascade on
this foundation; this chapter adds no `save_memory` tool or memory storage.

## Taking it for a spin

Use a scratch directory so a successful tool call changes a file you meant to
change. For a small demonstration, create these three files under its `skills`
directory. They form a separate example from the larger skill tree above.

`base/SKILL.md`:

```markdown
---
name: base
description: Small coding assistant
type: primary
tools: read_file
loadable-skills: code-tools
---
You are a concise coding assistant. Available tools: $TOOLS.
Skills you can load: $SKILLS.
```

`code-tools/SKILL.md`:

```markdown
---
name: code-tools
type: loadable
description: Write and verify a scratch file
tools: write_file
depends: helper
---
Write note.txt with content $CUSTOM_VAR using write_file, then use
read_file to verify it. Next available skills: $SKILLS.
```

`helper/SKILL.md`:

```markdown
---
name: helper
description: Scratch directory guidance
type: dependency
tools: list_directory
---
Work only in the current scratch directory.
```

Launch the built command from that scratch directory, with your chosen model
and provider credentials already configured in its environment:

```sh
EN_SKILLS_DIR=./skills EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=base EN_CUSTOM_VAR=SKILLS_OK /absolute/path/to/ensemble chat
```

Ask it to load `code-tools`, follow its instructions once, mark it for unload,
and answer with the verified file content. Inspect `note.txt` as well as the
answer. The load result should contain the helper's scratch-directory instruction
and the substituted marker; the next request should declare `write_file` and
`list_directory`. The system instructions should still be those rendered before
the first turn. Keep credentials out of any retained request capture.

The October 10, 2026 student sessions used discovered `claude-haiku-5-5`,
`gpt-4o-mini` and `gemini-3.8-flash` models. Each loaded this small skill graph
(the published examples add descriptions and wrap the body text),
wrote and read its own marker, marked `code-tools` pending unload and answered
with the file content. Each process exited normally. Their captured requests
retain identical system text within each session: five requests for the Claude
run, four for the OpenAI run and five for Gemini. These are historical run
identities; discover the models available to your account when repeating the
exercise. The [Claude](../solutions/evidence/ch10/anthropic-live.json),
[OpenAI](../solutions/evidence/ch10/openai-live.json) and
[Gemini](../solutions/evidence/ch10/gemini-live.json) receipts contain
the actual calls, results, file content and request bodies.

One successful run invited the wrong conclusion. The OpenAI session called
`unload_skill` before its final `read_file`, and the read succeeded. That looked
like proof that pending unload had retained the dynamic tools. But `read_file`
belonged to `base` all along. The read would have succeeded even if unload had
incorrectly disabled everything `code-tools` added.

The focused source test instead checks that the dynamically added `write_file`
remains declared after pending unload. Declaration and dispatch share the same
admission predicate, and restoring early removal makes that check fail. The
revised grader also exercises a dynamic write after marking unload. Match the
tool in the assertion to the capability whose lifetime is in question; another
successful paid run of the same read would prove no more.

The historical full grader was interrupted during its inherited GUI/headless
parity cascade and produced no aggregate score. Separate unchanged Skills phases
scored **65/85**, losing only the two declaration checks that required undefined
`think`; this was not a completed 65/100 run. The
[independent review](../docs/edition-2-notes/ch10-code-review.md) preserves
those results and their accepted exceptions. Edition 2's grader uses the
implemented tool set and the proper clients, with its new results recorded
separately in the [grader report](../docs/edition-2-notes/enhancement-09-code.md).

The agent can now acquire a manual and its tools without rewriting its
constitution. The next chapter gives the conversation a life beyond the
process that created it.
